::: {.lead}
*Harbor Guard* is a tower-defence game for phones. Ships sail into a harbour,
and the player taps a tile to build a tower. Before the game can draw one
picture, it must answer many questions with numbers: Where is each ship?
Which tile did the finger touch? How high is the tower? In this lesson you
learn why games need mathematics and how a **coordinate system** turns the
question "where is it?" into numbers. Every section ends with a short task:
on paper, in a free tool (GeoGebra or a spreadsheet) or in a mini-game.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary game-loop frame-rate coordinate-system origin axis coordinate ordered-pair quadrant screen-space world-space tile-grid handedness >}}

## 1.1 Mathematics in game development

For a computer, a game is a set of numbers in memory: the positions of the
characters, their health, the score, the time left. The game program repeats
three steps again and again:

1. read the player's input;
2. update the numbers by the rules of the game;
3. draw a picture of the new state on the screen.

This repeated cycle is the **game loop**. One pass through the loop makes one
picture, called a **frame** (@fig-game-loop).

![The game loop. One pass makes one frame. At 60 frames per second, the loop runs every 16.7 ms.](images/game-loop.png){#fig-game-loop width=78%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — Frame rate and frame time"}
The **frame rate** is the number of frames a game makes per second (frames
per second, fps). The **frame time** is the time for one frame:
$$\text{frame time} = \frac{1000}{\text{frame rate}} \text{ milliseconds (ms)}.$$
:::

The frame time is a strict limit. At 60 fps, the program has about 16.7 ms to
read the input, update every object and draw the picture. If it needs more
time, the frame is late and the game stutters. So game mathematics must be
correct and also fast: a few additions and multiplications per object per
frame.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — Frame budget"}
A racing game runs at 60 fps. A race lasts 3 minutes.

1. Frame time: $1000 / 60 \approx 16.7$ ms.
2. The race lasts $3 \times 60 = 180$ seconds.
3. Number of frames: $180 \times 60 = 10\,800$. The game updates the cars
   10 800 times.
4. On an old phone at 30 fps, each frame has $1000 / 30 \approx 33.3$ ms, and
   the race has only 5 400 frames. The cars move less smoothly.
:::

@tbl-map shows where the mathematics of this course appears in a game.

| What the game does | Mathematics | Weeks |
|---|---|---|
| Store where every object is; move it | coordinates, vectors | 1–3 |
| Aim a turret; make an object bob up and down | trigonometry | 4 |
| Move, turn and resize models; place the camera | matrices | 5–7 |
| Decide if a door opens or an enemy attacks | logic | 9–10 |
| Make loot, critical hits and random levels | probability | 11–13 |

: Mathematics behind common game tasks. {#tbl-map}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the mathematics in a game"}
Play a game on your phone for two minutes.

1. Write four things that the game must compute with numbers, for example
   "the position of my car" or "the chance of a rare item".
2. For each one, write the mathematics from @tbl-map that it needs.

*Your result:* a table with four rows: game thing, mathematics.
:::

## 1.2 One-dimensional coordinates

The simplest coordinate system is the **number line**. We choose one point,
the **origin**, and call it 0. We choose a unit of length and a positive
direction. Then every point on the line has one number, its **coordinate**:
how many units it is from the origin. Points on the negative side have
negative coordinates.

![A one-dimensional world: a runner game. The position along the track is one number, x.](images/number-line.png){#fig-number-line width=88%}

Games use two kinds of number line. In a board game, positions are
**discrete**: only whole numbers are allowed, and a piece is on square 3 or on
square 4, never between. In a physics game, positions are **continuous**: a
character can stand at $x = 3.27$. Game code stores whole numbers as `int` and
decimal numbers as `float`. (A `float` is less exact for very large numbers.
This is why big open-world games keep the player near the origin.)

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.2 — Displacement and distance on a line"}
An object moves from coordinate $a$ to coordinate $b$.
Its **displacement** is $b - a$ (end minus start). The sign shows the
direction: plus means the positive direction, minus the negative direction.
The **distance** is the size of the displacement, without the sign. A
distance is never negative.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — Back to the checkpoint"}
In the runner game of @fig-number-line, the player is at $x = 4$. The last
checkpoint is at $x = -3$. The player falls and goes back to the checkpoint.

1. Displacement: end minus start $= -3 - 4 = -7$. The minus sign means that
   the player moves to the left.
2. Distance: 7 units.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Mixing up displacement and distance. A displacement of $-7$ and a
displacement of $+7$ have the same distance: 7 units. A negative distance is
always an error.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A runner track on paper"}
1. Draw a number line from $-5$ to $10$.
2. Mark a coin at 6, a trap at $-2$ and the start at 0.
3. The player runs from the start to the coin, then falls back to the trap.
   Write the displacement and the distance of each move.

*Your result:* the drawing, two displacements and two distances.
:::

## 1.3 The two-dimensional coordinate system

A two-dimensional (2D) game world needs two numbers for each point. The
**Cartesian coordinate system** uses two number lines that cross at the
origin at a right angle. The horizontal line is the **x-axis**. The vertical
line is the **y-axis**. Usually, $x$ grows to the right and $y$ grows upward.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.3 — Ordered pair"}
A point in the plane is written as an **ordered pair** $(x, y)$. The first
number is the $x$-coordinate, the second number is the $y$-coordinate. The
order matters: $(3, 2)$ and $(2, 3)$ are different points.
:::

The two axes cut the plane into four **quadrants**, numbered I to IV
anticlockwise, starting at the top right (@fig-quadrants). The signs of the
coordinates tell the quadrant. A point with a zero coordinate lies on an axis
and is in no quadrant: $(5, 0)$ is on the $x$-axis, $(0, -2)$ is on the
$y$-axis.

![The four quadrants and their signs, with four game objects in a 2D level.](images/quadrants.png){#fig-quadrants width=58%}

| Quadrant | Sign of x | Sign of y | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | + | + | (4, 3) |
| II | − | + | (−3, 2) |
| III | − | − | (−4, −2.5) |
| IV | + | − | (2, −3) |

: Signs of the four quadrants. {#tbl-quadrants}

Level designers often put the origin at a useful place, for example the centre
of an arena or the start point of the player. Then negative coordinates are
normal: an enemy at $(-6, 1)$ is six units left of the centre and one unit up.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.3 — Reading positions in a level"}
In @fig-quadrants, the coin is at $(4, 3)$, the key at $(-3, 2)$, the trap at
$(-4, -2.5)$ and the exit at $(2, -3)$.

1. The key has $x < 0$ and $y > 0$: it is in quadrant II.
2. The trap has two negative coordinates: quadrant III.
3. From the key to the coin, $x$ changes from $-3$ to 4: that is 7 units to
   the right. $y$ changes from 2 to 3: 1 unit up.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Build the level in GeoGebra"}
Open the free GeoGebra calculator in a browser (geogebra.org/calculator; no
account is needed).

1. Type the four points of Example 1.3, one per line, for example
   `Coin = (4, 3)`.
2. Check that each point is in the quadrant of Example 1.3.
3. Add your own enemy in quadrant IV and a door on the y-axis.

*Your result:* the coordinates of your enemy and your door, and the quadrant
(or axis) of each.
:::

## 1.4 Screen space and world space

The coordinates of the game world are not the coordinates of the screen. A
screen is a grid of **pixels**, and pixels are counted from the **top-left
corner**. Screen $x$ grows to the right, but screen $y$ grows *downward*. A
phone of $1080 \times 1920$ pixels (portrait) has screen points from $(0, 0)$
at the top left to $(1079, 1919)$ at the bottom right.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.4 — World space and screen space"}
**World space** is the coordinate system of the game world. It uses world
units (often metres), $y$ grows upward, and the designer chooses the origin.
**Screen space** is the coordinate system of the display. It uses pixels,
the origin is the top-left corner, and $y$ grows downward.
:::

![The same point in world space (left) and in screen space (right). The camera shows the world origin in the centre of the screen.](images/screen-world.png){#fig-screen-world width=92%}

Suppose the camera shows the world origin in the centre of the screen, and
one world unit is drawn as $s$ pixels (the *scale*). For a screen $W$ pixels
wide and $H$ pixels high, the centre is at $(W/2, H/2)$, and:

$$x_s = \frac{W}{2} + s \cdot x_w, \qquad y_s = \frac{H}{2} - s \cdot y_w .$$

The minus sign turns $y$ around, because screen $y$ grows downward. A touch
game also needs the opposite direction: *the finger touched this pixel —
which point of the world is it?*

$$x_w = \frac{x_s - W/2}{s}, \qquad y_w = \frac{H/2 - y_s}{s} .$$

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.4 — From the world to the screen"}
A phone has $W = 1080$ and $H = 1920$ pixels, and the scale is $s = 100$ pixels
per unit. Where is the world point $(2, 3)$ on the screen?

1. Centre of the screen: $(540, 960)$.
2. $x_s = 540 + 100 \times 2 = 740$.
3. $y_s = 960 - 100 \times 3 = 660$.
4. The point is at pixel $(740, 660)$: right of the centre and *above* it,
   because 660 is smaller than 960.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.5 — From a touch to the world"}
On the same phone, the player touches the pixel $(340, 1160)$.

1. $x_w = (340 - 540) / 100 = -200 / 100 = -2$.
2. $y_w = (960 - 1160) / 100 = -200 / 100 = -2$.
3. The player touched the world point $(-2, -2)$, in quadrant III.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.6 — Which part of the world can the player see?"}
On the same phone ($1080 \times 1920$, $s = 100$), which world points are at
the corners of the screen?

1. Top-left pixel $(0, 0)$: $x_w = (0 - 540) / 100 = -5.4$ and
   $y_w = (960 - 0) / 100 = 9.6$. World point $(-5.4, 9.6)$.
2. Bottom-right pixel $(1080, 1920)$: $x_w = 5.4$ and $y_w = -9.6$.
3. So the player sees the world from $x = -5.4$ to $5.4$ and from
   $y = -9.6$ to $9.6$. A ship at $(7, 2)$ is outside the screen: the game
   does not need to draw it.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Forgetting that screen $y$ grows downward. With a plus instead of the minus
in the formula for $y_s$, the whole world is drawn upside down: a character
that jumps seems to fall.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/grid-strike.html" poster="sims/grid-strike.png" title="Grid Strike: hit the coordinates" kind="game" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Grid Strike"}
Open the **Grid Strike** mini-game above (or scan its QR code). Stage 1 uses
world coordinates. Stage 2 uses screen coordinates, with $y$ growing downward.

1. Play both stages.
2. Write your score in each stage, and one point you missed.

*Your result:* two scores, and one sentence: why is stage 2 harder at first?
:::

## 1.5 Grids and tile maps

Many mobile games are built on a **grid**: puzzle boards, tile maps,
inventories. On a grid, a position is a pair of whole numbers: the **column**
$c$ and the **row** $r$, both counted from 0.

Computer memory is one long list. So a grid is stored row after row, as one
list. This is called **row-major order** (@fig-tile-index).

![A board of 8 columns stored row after row. Each cell has a pair (c, r) and one index i.](images/tile-index.png){#fig-tile-index width=80%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.5 — Index of a cell"}
On a grid with $n$ columns, the cell in column $c$ and row $r$ has the index
$$i = r \times n + c .$$
In the other direction: divide the index $i$ by $n$. The whole-number result is
the row $r$, and the remainder is the column $c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.7 — A match-3 board"}
A match-3 board has $n = 8$ columns.

1. The gem in column 5, row 3: $i = 3 \times 8 + 5 = 29$.
2. The gem with index 42: $42 \div 8 = 5$, remainder 2. So it is in row 5,
   column 2.
3. One cell to the right has index $42 + 1 = 43$. One row up has index
   $42 + 8 = 50$: moving one row changes the index by $n$.
:::

To place an object *on* a tile, the game needs the centre of the tile in
world space. If each tile is $t$ units wide, row 0 is at the bottom and the
grid starts at the world origin, the centre of tile $(c, r)$ is
$$x = (c + 0.5) \times t, \qquad y = (r + 0.5) \times t .$$

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.8 — A tower in the middle of its tile"}
Tiles are 2 units wide. The player builds a tower on tile $(3, 1)$.

1. $x = (3 + 0.5) \times 2 = 7$.
2. $y = (1 + 0.5) \times 2 = 3$.
3. The game places the tower at $(7, 3)$, the centre of the tile, not at its
   corner $(6, 2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
A short C# example to read. In C#, `/` between two whole numbers keeps only
the whole-number part, and `%` gives the remainder.

```csharp
int columns = 8;
int index = 42;
int column = index % columns;   // 2
int row = index / columns;      // 5
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A board in a spreadsheet"}
Open a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets).

1. Make a board of 5 columns and 4 rows. Type the index of each cell, row
   after row: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 in the first row, 5 to 9 in the second row, and so
   on.
2. Choose three cells. For each one, check $i = r \times 5 + c$.

*Your result:* the board, and your three checks.
:::

## 1.6 The three-dimensional coordinate system

A three-dimensional (3D) world adds a third axis, the **z-axis**, at a right
angle to both other axes. A point is now an **ordered triple** $(x, y, z)$. In
a world where $y$ points up, the ground is flat on the $x$ and $z$ axes, and
the $y$-coordinate is the height above the ground. Every point with $y = 0$
is on the ground.

### Left-handed and right-handed

When $x$ points right and $y$ points up, the $z$-axis can point *into* the
screen or *out of* it. This gives two systems. Use your hand to tell them
apart: point your thumb along $+x$ and your index finger along $+y$. Bend your
middle finger: it points along $+z$. If this works with the left hand, the
system is **left-handed**. If it works with the right hand, it is
**right-handed** (@fig-handedness).

![Left-handed (left) and right-handed (right) systems, with x to the right and y up.](images/handedness.png){#fig-handedness width=86%}

Game tools do not agree. Two tools that game developers use every day:

| Software | Up axis | Handedness |
|---|---|---|
| Unity (game engine) | $y$ | left-handed |
| Blender (3D modelling) | $z$ | right-handed |

: Coordinate systems of two common tools. {#tbl-conventions}

To move a position from Blender to Unity, swap the last two numbers:
$(x, y, z)$ in Blender becomes $(x, z, y)$ in Unity.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.9 — From Blender to Unity"}
A designer places a lamp at $(1, 4, 2)$ in Blender ($z$ up).

1. In Blender, the height is the $z$-coordinate: 2 units.
2. Swap the last two numbers: the lamp is at $(1, 2, 4)$ in Unity.
3. Check: in Unity the height is the $y$-coordinate, 2. The lamp is still
   2 units above the ground.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
In C#, the type `Vector3` holds three decimal numbers, $x$, $y$ and $z$. The
letter `f` marks a decimal (`float`) number.

```csharp
Vector3 lamp = new Vector3(1f, 2f, 4f);   // x = 1, y = 2 (height), z = 4
float height = lamp.y;                     // 2
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Copying positions from another tool without checking its axes. A model from
Blender put into Unity without the swap stands on its side or appears in the
wrong place.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/position-3d.html" poster="images/axes-3d.png" title="Place an object in 3D" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Move a player in 3D"}
Open the 3D viewer above (or scan its QR code). Drag to turn the world.

1. Move the player to $(1, 2, 4)$ with the sliders. Which slider changes the
   height?
2. Catch three coins. Write the coordinates of each coin.

*Your result:* the slider for the height, and three coordinates $(x, y, z)$.
:::

## Case study: where the mathematics is in Harbor Guard

*Harbor Guard* is a made-up tower-defence game for phones in portrait
($1080 \times 1920$ pixels). The harbour is a grid of 9 columns of tiles, each
1 unit wide. The camera shows the world origin in the centre of the screen,
with a scale of 120 pixels per unit. Ships sail in from the top of the
screen, and the player taps a tile to build a tower. The game runs at 60 fps.
In the 3D version, the towers are models made in Blender. Each sentence hides
one idea of this lesson: frame time (1.1), coordinates and quadrants (1.3),
from a touch to the world (1.4), the index of a tile (1.5) and moving models
between tools (1.6). The Game challenge of the interactive lesson works
through it.

![A screen of Harbor Guard. The game must find the tapped tile (red) from the pixel that the finger touched.](images/harbor-guard.png){#fig-harbor width=46%}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapter 1 ("Cartesian Coordinate Systems"): 1D mathematics, 2D and 3D
Cartesian space, and left- and right-handed coordinate spaces.

## Exercises

1. A game runs at 50 fps. What is the frame time in milliseconds?
2. A game runs at 60 fps for 2 minutes. How many frames is that?
3. On a number line, a platform moves from $x = -2$ to $x = 6$. Write its
   displacement and its distance.
4. In which quadrant, or on which axis, is each point: $(-7, 3)$, $(0, -4)$,
   $(5, -1)$, $(-1, -1)$, $(8, 0)$?
5. The player is at $(-3, 4)$ and an enemy at $(5, 4)$. How far apart are
   they? Why is the vertical difference not needed?
6. A phone has $W = 1080$, $H = 1920$ and $s = 100$. Where on the screen is the
   world point $(-1, 2)$?
7. On the same phone, the player touches the pixel $(840, 760)$. Which world
   point was touched? In which quadrant is it?
8. A game draws a point with $y_w = 4$ *below* the centre of the screen. What
   is wrong in its formula?
9. An inventory has 6 columns. Find the index of the slot in column 4, row 2.
10. On the same inventory, in which column and row is index 23?
11. In a $y$-up world, a drone is at $(4, 12, -3)$. How high is it? Which
    number changes if it lands straight down?
12. A model is at $(2, -5, 3)$ in Blender. Where is it in Unity?
13. *Harbor Guard*: the player taps the pixel $(780, 840)$. Which world point
    is it, and in which quadrant?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. 1000 / 50 = 20 ms.
2. 2 × 60 = 120 seconds; 120 × 60 = 7 200 frames.
3. Displacement 6 − (−2) = 8; distance 8 units.
4. II; on the y-axis; IV; III; on the x-axis.
5. 5 − (−3) = 8 units; both have y = 4, so the vertical difference is 0.
6. x = 540 + 100 × (−1) = 440; y = 960 − 100 × 2 = 760: pixel (440, 760).
7. x = (840 − 540) / 100 = 3; y = (960 − 760) / 100 = 2: point (3, 2), quadrant I.
8. It adds s × y instead of subtracting it; screen y grows downward.
9. 2 × 6 + 4 = 16.
10. 23 ÷ 6 = 3, remainder 5: column 5, row 3.
11. 12 units; only y changes (to 0).
12. (2, 3, −5).
13. x = (780 − 540) / 120 = 2; y = (960 − 840) / 120 = 1: point (2, 1), quadrant I.
:::
